Deniz held Grandpa's hand on the garden path. Little white stones showed where to walk. Soon they reached the observation shelter, a small wooden roof with open sides. Deniz looked at the pool. The water did not reach the painted stone marker! Usually the water touched the white line. Deniz leaned close and looked and looked. "Why is it lower?" Deniz asked. Grandpa smiled. "Let's look together and find out."

From the shelter, Deniz watched the water. It was very still. It sat lower than the tall green reeds at the edge. A little insect skated across the top. Another one rested on a leaf. The reeds swayed in the breeze, just like always. "The water is quiet today," Deniz said. Grandpa knelt down. "What else do you see?" Deniz squinted. Then Deniz remembered a puddle from before, a puddle that got smaller and smaller in the sunshine.

"It has been sunny a lot," Deniz said. "No rain for lots of days." Grandpa nodded. "Yes, many warm, dry days this week." Deniz thought about that little puddle. After one sunny afternoon, it got smaller. "Maybe the sun drank some water," Deniz said. Then Deniz paused and shook a small finger. "But that puddle was little. This pool is big. Maybe is not the same as know." Grandpa chuckled. "Good thinking. Maybe is a fine place to start."

Deniz walked a little way along the marked path, with Grandpa right beside. Near the end of the pool was a small metal grate where water could come in. Leaves and twigs had gathered there in a little pile. "Look! Leaves and sticks by the gate," Deniz said. "Maybe the water cannot come in good." Then Deniz noticed the plants. Some leaves were yellow and orange now, not all green. "The leaves changed too," Deniz said slowly. "But maybe that is not why the water is low. Leaves just change when the season turns."

Deniz counted on small fingers. "One. Sunny days make water smaller. Two. Leaves and sticks sit by the gate. Three. Leaves are turning colors." Deniz shook a head. "I don't know which one did it. Maybe all. Maybe some." Grandpa nodded. "What gentle thing can we do?" Deniz looked at the grate but did not touch it. "Tell the gardener! Tell her about the leaves and sticks and the water line." So Grandpa found Ms. Rosa, the community gardener, and told her exactly what they had seen, so she could check the grate safely.

Deniz and Grandpa stood on the marked path and watched. Ms. Rosa put on tall boots and checked the inlet grate, carefully, all by herself. She nodded and wrote on her clipboard. The pool was still low. But a bird sang from far away, insects buzzed, and the reeds swayed in the wind, just as they always did. "We looked, we told, and we can look again," Deniz said. Grandpa squeezed Deniz's hand. "Next time we visit, we will see what changed." Deniz smiled big. Looking again was a good way to help.

Su Kenarındaki Değişiklik

Deniz, bahçe yolunda Dede’sinin elini tuttu. Küçük beyaz taşlar nereden yürüneceğini gösteriyordu. Sonunda gözlem kulübesine vardılar. Burası, yanları açık, küçük ahşap çatılı bir yerdi. Deniz gölete baktı. Su, boyalı işaret taşına kadar gelmemişti! Normalde su beyaz çizgiye değiyordu. Deniz yaklaşıp uzun uzun baktı.

“Su neden daha aşağıda?” diye sordu Deniz.

Dede gülümsedi.

“Birlikte bakalım ve öğrenelim,” dedi.

Deniz, kulübeden suyu izledi. Su çok sakindi. Kıyıdaki uzun yeşil sazlardan daha aşağıdaydı. Küçük bir böcek suyun üstünde kayarak ilerledi. Bir başkası da bir yaprağın üzerinde durdu. Sazlar, her zamanki gibi, rüzgârda sallanıyordu.

“Su bugün çok sessiz,” dedi Deniz.

Dede diz çöktü.

“Başka ne görüyorsun?”

Deniz gözlerini kıstı. Sonra daha önce gördüğü bir su birikintisini hatırladı. O su birikintisi güneşte gittikçe küçülmüştü.

“Hava çok güneşliydi,” dedi Deniz. “Birçok gündür yağmur yağmadı.”

Dede başını salladı.

“Evet, bu hafta birçok sıcak ve kuru gün oldu.”

Deniz o küçük su birikintisini düşündü. Güneşli bir öğleden sonra onun küçüldüğünü hatırladı.

“Belki güneş biraz su içmiştir,” dedi Deniz.

Sonra durdu ve küçük parmağını salladı.

“Ama o su birikintisi küçüktü. Bu gölet büyük. Belki aynı şey değildir.”

Dede kıkırdadı.

“İyi düşündün. ‘Belki’ demek başlamak için güzel bir yerdir.”

Deniz, Dede’si hemen yanında yürürken işaretli yol boyunca biraz ilerledi. Göletin sonuna yakın, suyun içeri girebileceği küçük bir metal ızgara vardı. Yapraklar ve dallar orada küçük bir yığın oluşturmuştu.

“Bak! Izgaranın yanında yapraklar ve dallar var,” dedi Deniz. “Belki su içeri iyi giremiyordur.”

Sonra Deniz bitkileri fark etti. Bazı yapraklar artık tamamen yeşil değildi; sarı ve turuncu olmuşlardı.

“Yapraklar da değişmiş,” dedi Deniz yavaşça. “Ama belki suyun azalmasının nedeni bu değildir. Mevsim değişince yapraklar renk değiştirir.”

Deniz küçük parmaklarıyla saydı.

“Bir. Güneşli günler suyu azaltıyor. İki. Yapraklar ve dallar ızgaranın yanında duruyor. Üç. Yaprakların renkleri değişiyor.”

Deniz başını salladı.

“Hangisinin yaptığını bilmiyorum. Belki hepsi. Belki bazıları.”

Dede başını salladı.

“Kimseye zarar vermeden ne yapabiliriz?”

Deniz ızgaraya baktı ama ona dokunmadı.

“Bahçıvana söyleyelim! Yaprakları, dalları ve su çizgisini anlatalım.”

Böylece Dede, mahalle bahçıvanı Rosa Hanım’ı buldu ve gördüklerini ona aynen anlattı. Rosa Hanım da ızgarayı güvenle kontrol edebilecekti.

Deniz ve Dede, işaretli yolun üzerinde durup izlediler. Rosa Hanım uzun çizmelerini giydi ve su girişindeki ızgarayı tek başına, dikkatlice kontrol etti. Başını salladı ve not defterine yazdı.

Göletin suyu hâlâ alçaktı. Ama uzaktan bir kuş ötüyor, böcekler vızıldıyor ve sazlar her zamanki gibi rüzgârda sallanıyordu.

“Baktık, haber verdik ve yine bakabiliriz,” dedi Deniz.

Dede, Deniz’in elini sıktı.

“Bir dahaki gelişimizde neyin değiştiğini görürüz.”

Deniz kocaman gülümsedi. Yeniden bakmak, yardım etmenin iyi bir yoluydu.

candidates.english_story:
Deniz held Papa's hand and walked the little path to the wetland shelter. It was their favorite spot to look at the water. But today, the shallow pool looked strange. It did not touch the painted stone marker like it always did. The water sat lower, with a thin ring of dry mud around the edge. Deniz stopped and pointed. "Papa, why is it lower?" Papa looked too. "I don't know yet," he said softly. "Let's look closely."

Deniz remembered last time, the water had reached right up to the painted stone. It had been shiny and full. Now there was space between the stone and the water. Deniz remembered something else too. One sunny day, a puddle by the swings had gotten smaller and smaller after the sun stayed out all afternoon. This week had been warm, with lots of sunny days in a row. "Maybe the warm sun changed some water," Deniz said carefully. Papa nodded. "That could be part of it. Let's keep looking."

From the path, Deniz looked toward the reed edge. There, by a small metal grate, leaves and twigs had gathered in a little pile. The grate let water flow in and out. Deniz did not touch it, just looked. Nearby, some plants had turned yellow and orange, the way they did every year at this time. A dragonfly zipped past. Two birds pecked calmly near the shallow edge. Everything seemed busy and ordinary. Deniz remembered not to go near the thick reeds where nests might be hiding. "There's a lot to see," Deniz said.

Sitting on the shelter bench, Deniz thought hard. "Maybe the dry days made the water lower," Deniz said. "And maybe the leaves and twigs are blocking the little grate too." Papa asked, "What about the yellow leaves on the plants?" Deniz shook their head. "Those just mean it's a different season. They don't tell us why the water is lower." Papa smiled. "That's good thinking. What can we do?" Deniz thought a moment. "We can't fix the sun. But we can tell the caretaker about the grate."

They found the caretaker near the garden shed. "Leaves and twigs are by the little grate," Deniz said. "The water is lower too." The caretaker smiled and thanked Deniz for noticing. Together, they walked to the public-side grate. Carefully, the caretaker lifted out the loose leaves and twigs, just from the opening. She left the reeds alone and did not step into the water. "This might help a little," she said. "But the dry weather matters too. We'll keep watching."

Deniz looked once more at the pool from the path. The water was still lower than the painted stone. The plants stayed yellow and orange in the sunlight. Little insects buzzed near the reeds, and a bird splashed in the shallow water, unbothered. "Maybe the grate helped some," Deniz said, "and maybe the sun and season matter too. We don't know everything yet." Papa squeezed Deniz's hand. "That's okay. We can look again next time." Deniz smiled, already wondering what they might notice on their next visit.

“Bakacak çok şey var,” dedi Deniz.

Deniz, kulübenin sırasına oturup iyice düşündü.

“Belki kurak günler suyun alçalmasına neden oldu,” dedi Deniz. “Belki yapraklar ve ince dallar küçük ızgarayı da tıkıyordur.”

Baba sordu:

“Peki bitkilerdeki sarı yapraklar?”

Deniz başını salladı.

“Onlar sadece mevsimin değiştiğini gösteriyor. Suyun neden alçaldığını anlatmıyorlar.”

Baba gülümsedi.

“İyi düşündün. Ne yapabiliriz?”

Deniz bir süre düşündü.

“Güneşi düzeltemeyiz. Ama ızgarayı görevliye söyleyebiliriz.”

Bahçe kulübesinin yanında görevli kadını buldular.

“Küçük ızgaranın yanında yapraklar ve ince dallar var,” dedi Deniz. “Su da daha alçak.”

Görevli kadın gülümsedi ve fark ettiği için Deniz’e teşekkür etti. Sonra birlikte, halka açık taraftaki ızgaraya gittiler. Görevli kadın, sadece girişteki gevşek yaprakları ve ince dalları dikkatlice çıkardı. Sazlıklara dokunmadı ve suya girmedi.

“Bu biraz yardımcı olabilir,” dedi. “Ama kuru havanın da etkisi var. Bakmaya devam edeceğiz.”

Deniz, patikadan su birikintisine bir kez daha baktı. Su hâlâ boyalı taştan daha alçaktı. Bitkiler güneş ışığında sarı ve turuncu kalmıştı. Küçük böcekler sazlıkların yanında vızıldıyor, bir kuş da sığ suda rahatsız olmadan suya girip çıkıyordu.

“Belki ızgara biraz yardımcı oldu,” dedi Deniz, “belki güneşin ve mevsimin de etkisi var. Henüz her şeyi bilmiyoruz.”

Baba, Deniz’in elini sıktı.

“Bu sorun değil. Bir dahaki gelişimizde yine bakabiliriz.”

Deniz gülümsedi. Bir sonraki ziyaretlerinde neleri fark edebileceklerini şimdiden merak ediyordu.

scenes.prose: Deniz held Papa's hand and walked the little path to the wetland shelter. It was their favorite spot to look at the water. But today, the shallow pool looked strange. It did not touch the painted stone marker like it always did. The water sat lower, with a thin ring of dry mud around the edge. Deniz stopped and pointed. "Papa, why is it lower?" Papa looked too. "I don't know yet," he said softly. "Let's look closely."

Deniz remembered last time, the water had reached right up to the painted stone. It had been shiny and full. Now there was space between the stone and the water. Deniz remembered something else too. One sunny day, a puddle by the swings had gotten smaller and smaller after the sun stayed out all afternoon. This week had been warm, with lots of sunny days in a row. "Maybe the warm sun changed some water," Deniz said carefully. Papa nodded. "That could be part of it. Let's keep looking."

From the path, Deniz looked toward the reed edge. There, by a small metal grate, leaves and twigs had gathered in a little pile. The grate let water flow in and out. Deniz did not touch it, just looked. Nearby, some plants had turned yellow and orange, the way they did every year at this time. A dragonfly zipped past. Two birds pecked calmly near the shallow edge. Everything seemed busy and ordinary. Deniz remembered not to go near the thick reeds where nests might be hiding. "There's a lot to see," Deniz said.

Sitting on the shelter bench, Deniz thought hard. "Maybe the dry days made the water lower," Deniz said. "And maybe the leaves and twigs are blocking the little grate too." Papa asked, "What about the yellow leaves on the plants?" Deniz shook their head. "Those just mean it's a different season. They don't tell us why the water is lower." Papa smiled. "That's good thinking. What can we do?" Deniz thought a moment. "We can't fix the sun. But we can tell the caretaker about the grate."

They found the caretaker near the garden shed. "Leaves and twigs are by the little grate," Deniz said. "The water is lower too." The caretaker smiled and thanked Deniz for noticing. Together, they walked to the public-side grate. Carefully, the caretaker lifted out the loose leaves and twigs, just from the opening. She left the reeds alone and did not step into the water. "This might help a little," she said. "But the dry weather matters too. We'll keep watching."

Deniz looked once more at the pool from the path. The water was still lower than the painted stone. The plants stayed yellow and orange in the sunlight. Little insects buzzed near the reeds, and a bird splashed in the shallow water, unbothered. "Maybe the grate helped some," Deniz said, "and maybe the sun and season matter too. We don't know everything yet." Papa squeezed Deniz's hand. "That's okay. We can look again next time." Deniz smiled, already wondering what they might notice on their next visit.

final_judge.summary: ACCEPT. This story meets all acceptance criteria with exceptional execution. The prose demonstrates mastery of the target age (4 years old, READ_ALOUD mode) through sentence rhythm, vocabulary precision, and emotional pacing. Deniz's reasoning is age-plausible: simple comparisons (puddle memory), cautious language ('maybe'), and concrete observations without independent action. All six scenes follow the SceneGraph beats precisely. The three required ecological clues appear clearly: lower water level, leaves/twigs at inlet grate, and seasonal plant color. The causal chain remains appropriately uncertain—weather, blockage, and season are all possible, none proven. The final action (caretaker clears public-side grate only) is proportionate, low-impact, and supervised. No prohibited knowledge leaks occur; the reed bed remains unexplored and its contents unknown. The ending preserves uncertainty ('We don't know everything yet') while affirming the value of repeated observation, matching the theme thread exactly. Vocabulary, sentence structure, and concept complexity are calibrated precisely to age 4: 'thin ring of dry mud,' 'zipped past,' 'unbothered,' 'squeezed Deniz's hand.' The adult (Papa) supports but does not solve. No catastrophe, fear, slogans, or magical thinking appear. Continuity across all six scenes is seamless. The story respects the wetland as an active ecosystem, not a teaching prop. Creativity is solid (the dragonfly, the bird splashing, the shelter bench scene) without overshadowing the core observational mission. This is production-ready work.
